blocks.text: **The task.** Given strings `s` and `t`, find the shortest substring of `s` containing every character of `t`, including duplicates. Return an empty string if none exists.
`"BANC"` holds A, B and C. It is shorter than `"ADOBEC"`, which also qualifies.

Validity is no longer a single number. We need **counts**: if `t` is `"AABC"`, the window needs two A's, not one. Tracking that naively means comparing two maps on every step, which would cost O(alphabet) per iteration.
Instead of comparing maps, keep a single integer `missing` — how many characters from `t` the window still lacks, counting duplicates.
The window is valid exactly when `missing === 0`. That reduces the validity check to a single comparison.
This is the elegant part. Every character in the window decrements its count, even characters not in `t`. So:

items: **Positive count** — the window still needs this many more.
**Negative** — the window has surplus copies it could afford to drop.

blocks.text: `missing` only changes when a count crosses the zero boundary, which is why `if (need.get(ch) > 0)` guards both the decrement and the increment. Surplus characters never affect validity.
**Time: O(|s| + |t|)** — each character of `s` enters and leaves once.
This problem combines everything in the chapter: a variable window, the shortest-variant recording position, and non-trivial state. If you can write it unaided, you have the pattern.
